units.sourceHTML: Functions
units.originalInnerHTML: Functions

units.sourceHTML:
Like many languages today, functions in Wren are little bundles of code 
you can store in a variable, or pass as an argument to a method.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Like many languages today, functions in Wren are little bundles of code 
you can store in a variable, or pass as an argument to a method.

units.sourceHTML: Notice there’s a difference between function and method.
units.originalInnerHTML: Notice there’s a difference between function and method.

units.sourceHTML:
Since Wren is object-oriented, most of your code will live in methods on
classes, but free-floating functions are still eminently handy.
units.originalInnerHTML:
Since Wren is object-oriented, most of your code will live in methods on
classes, but free-floating functions are still eminently handy.

units.sourceHTML:
Functions are objects like everything else in Wren, instances of the ⟦CODE0⟧
class.
units.originalInnerHTML: Functions are objects like everything else in Wren, instances of the Fn class.

units.sourceHTML: Creating a function #
units.originalInnerHTML: Creating a function #

units.sourceHTML:
To create a function, we call ⟦CODE0⟧, which takes a block to execute.
To call the function, we use ⟦CODE1⟧ on the function instance.
units.originalInnerHTML: To create a function, we call Fn.new, which takes a block to execute. To call the function, we use .call() on the function instance.

units.sourceHTML: Note that we’ll see a shorthand syntax for creating a function below.
units.originalInnerHTML: Note that we’ll see a shorthand syntax for creating a function below.

units.sourceHTML: Callable classes #
units.originalInnerHTML: Callable classes #

units.sourceHTML:
Because ⟦CODE0⟧ is a class, and responds to ⟦CODE1⟧, any class can respond to 
⟦CODE2⟧ and be used in place of a function. This is particularly handy when 
the function is passed to a method to be called, like a callback or event.
units.originalInnerHTML: Because Fn is a class, and responds to call(), any class can respond to call() and be used in place of a function. This is particularly handy when the function is passed to a method to be called, like a callback or event.
